Family Health

Bleeding after sex: causes, checks and treatment

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Bleeding during or after vaginal sex is often called postcoital bleeding. Common explanations include dryness, irritation, infection and changes on the cervix, but the cause cannot be identified from the amount or colour alone. Arrange a medical check even if the bleeding is light or stops quickly. Any bleeding after menopause needs assessment, and heavy bleeding or bleeding with severe pain or faintness may need urgent care.

Where the blood may be coming from

Blood noticed after sex may come from the vaginal wall, cervix or uterus, or from an injury around the vulva and labia. Occasionally blood from the urinary tract or another nearby area is mistaken for vaginal bleeding. Finding the source helps determine the right tests.

The cervix is the opening of the uterus at the top of the vagina. Contact can make a delicate or inflamed area on its surface bleed. After menopause, changes in the vaginal lining and conditions affecting the uterine lining also become important possibilities.

Spotting is a small amount of blood, sometimes seen only on tissue or underwear. A larger amount, repeated episodes or bleeding between periods adds useful information, but a small amount does not reliably exclude a condition that needs treatment.

You do not need to work out the anatomical source before asking for help. A clinician can review the timing, symptoms and examination findings without assuming that sex itself explains every episode.

Infection and inflammation

Infection can make tissue more sensitive and likely to bleed when touched. Cervicitis means inflammation of the cervix; vaginitis means inflammation of the vagina. These terms describe the affected area and do not by themselves identify a particular infection.

Sexually transmitted infections such as chlamydia can cause bleeding, and pelvic inflammatory disease may also be relevant, especially with pelvic pain or other symptoms. Some infections produce few obvious symptoms, so the absence of a strong smell or itching does not rule them out.

Tell the clinician about unusual discharge, pain during sex, burning when passing urine, itching, fever or lower abdominal pain. Questions about partners, barrier use and possible exposure help select tests and treatment. They should be asked respectfully and confidentially.

Not every inflamed or sore vagina needs antibiotics. Dryness, irritation and other noninfectious causes can produce similar symptoms. Treatment should follow the diagnosis, and some diagnosed STIs also require partner testing or treatment.

Menopause and genitourinary symptoms

Lower oestrogen around and after menopause can change the vagina and nearby urinary tissues. The term genitourinary syndrome of menopause, or GSM, includes symptoms such as dryness, irritation, discomfort during sex and some urinary problems. It was previously often described as vaginal atrophy.

The vaginal lining may become thinner, less elastic and more easily irritated. Less lubrication and fragile tissue can lead to soreness or small breaks during penetration. Similar hormone-related changes can follow removal of both ovaries or some cancer treatments.

These symptoms are treatable and are not something you have to tolerate as the inevitable price of ageing. However, bleeding should be assessed before it is attributed to GSM. A familiar feeling of dryness does not prove that dryness is the only cause.

Bleeding after menopause needs a check even if it happened only once, followed sex or appeared as a small pink or brown stain. In this setting, assessment also considers the uterine lining, not only the cervix or vaginal surface.

Other reasons for vaginal dryness

Dryness can occur before menopause, including after childbirth and during breastfeeding. Some medicines, such as certain antidepressants, hormonal medicines and treatments that reduce oestrogen, may contribute. Chemotherapy, pelvic radiotherapy and surgery can also affect comfort and lubrication.

If symptoms began after a medicine change, ask a clinician or pharmacist to review it. Do not stop a prescribed treatment without advice. A general list of cold, asthma or other medicines cannot establish that a particular product is the cause.

Arousal-related lubrication varies. Penetration before you feel ready or sufficiently lubricated can increase friction, but pain or dryness should not be framed as a failure to relax. Allowing more time and using suitable lubrication may help while persistent symptoms are assessed.

Douching and fragranced intimate washes can irritate the area. Some people are sensitive to detergents or other products. Conditions such as Sjögren’s syndrome can reduce moisture in the body and may contribute to vaginal dryness. Mention symptoms elsewhere or a known diagnosis to your clinician.

Polyps and cervical ectropion

Polyps are small growths that can occur on the cervix or inside the uterus. Many are benign, but they should not be declared harmless solely from symptoms. Their delicate blood vessels can bleed, including after contact.

A clinician may recommend removing a symptomatic polyp or checking tissue, depending on its location and your circumstances. You cannot confirm or treat a polyp at home, and not every episode of spotting comes from one.

Another common cause is cervical ectropion, in which delicate glandular cells from inside the cervical canal are visible on its outer surface. It can look red and may bleed after contact or produce more discharge. Ectropion itself is a benign change, not cervical cancer.

Before treating troublesome ectropion, clinicians check for infection and other abnormalities. It is important to distinguish this from the idea that an infection has damaged cells that must simply be burned or frozen away.

Friction, small tears and injury

Friction during penetration can cause small scratches or tears, particularly when tissue is dry or less elastic. Forceful activity can make this more likely. Pain or bleeding is a reason to stop and assess what is happening, not to push through.

A small injury may settle, but bleeding after sex should still be discussed with a clinician, especially if it recurs or its source is uncertain. Deep pain, persistent bleeding or an injury that appears significant needs prompt assessment.

For future sexual contact, choose a comfortable pace and activity, communicate about discomfort and use an appropriate lubricant if needed. Penetration is optional; it should never be continued because a partner expects it.

If the contact was unwanted or forced, you can seek medical care and confidential support. An examination and treatment should respect your choices and need for safety.

Could it be cancer?

Most bleeding after sex has a noncancerous explanation, but it can be a symptom of cervical or vaginal cancer. Bleeding after menopause can also be associated with cancer of the uterine lining. This possibility is why checking symptoms matters even when the bleeding seems minor.

Cervical cancer can occur well before fifty and should not be treated as exclusively a postmenopausal disease. Persistent infection with certain high-risk HPV types is its main cause, and smoking is one of the factors that can increase risk.

Endometrial cancer is more common after menopause. Relevant risk factors can include higher body weight, particular hormone exposures and some inherited or family cancer histories. These factors guide assessment; they do not tell you that a current episode is cancer.

A normal screening result or a history of HPV vaccination does not replace evaluation of a new symptom. Do not wait until your next routine screening invitation. Early identification of a serious cause can make a meaningful difference to treatment.

When to seek care and when it is urgent

Book a primary-care, gynaecology or sexual-health appointment for bleeding after sex, including light spotting. Be clear if you have reached menopause, if pregnancy is possible, or if the bleeding has happened more than once.

Seek urgent help for heavy or ongoing bleeding, severe abdominal or pelvic pain, faintness, collapse or feeling acutely unwell. Fever with pelvic pain or unusual discharge also needs prompt assessment. The urgency depends on the whole picture, not simply whether the blood looks fresh.

A missed period together with unusual bleeding and abdominal pain needs urgent assessment for possible ectopic pregnancy. If you are pregnant, contact your maternity or pregnancy-care service for advice about bleeding rather than assuming sex has made it harmless.

Mention associated itching, burning, painful urination, painful sex, lower back pain, nausea or vomiting. These symptoms can help identify infection, injury or another condition, although none points to a single cause on its own.

What happens at the appointment

The clinician usually asks when the bleeding started, how much there was, whether it happened during or after sex and whether it occurs at other times. Details about periods, menopause, pregnancy possibility, contraception, medicines and previous procedures also help.

You may be asked about your sexual history and previous screening or STI tests. These questions are intended to guide care, not to assign blame. Say if a question is unclear or if you need to discuss it privately.

An examination may include the vulva and an internal view of the vaginal walls and cervix using a speculum. This can identify a visible tear, polyp, inflamed area or other change. Depending on symptoms, the clinician may also check for tenderness or a possible urinary source.

Initial tests may include a pregnancy test, STI testing from a swab or urine sample, and blood tests when the amount or duration of bleeding suggests they would help. Not everyone needs every test, and the sequence depends on the findings.

If an examination worries you

Tell the service when booking if you are anxious, have experienced pain during an examination or have a history that makes it difficult. You can begin with a conversation about what the clinician recommends and why.

Ask for each step to be explained, a suitable chaperone or support person, a pause if needed and adjustments that may improve comfort. You can ask whether a smaller speculum or a different position is suitable. Consent remains yours throughout.

Some initial information can be obtained from a discussion, urine testing or, where appropriate and available, a self-collected swab. These options do not always replace an examination when the cervix or vaginal walls need to be seen.

It would be misleading to promise that assessment never needs a pelvic examination. The aim is to plan necessary care in a way you can manage, rather than letting fear of one part of the visit prevent you from seeking help at all.

Further tests and why a smear is not enough

Routine cervical screening is designed to identify HPV-related risk and precancerous changes. It is not a complete diagnostic test for bleeding and does not assess every part of the vagina or uterus. A normal result cannot rule out every relevant disease.

A colposcopy uses magnification to examine the cervix more closely and may include a small biopsy. Ultrasound can assess the uterus and other pelvic structures. Hysteroscopy allows a clinician to look inside the uterine cavity, sometimes with tissue sampling.

For postmenopausal bleeding, current local pathways determine the initial tests. ACOG’s April 2026 update recommends a combination of transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial tissue sampling for most patients, rather than relying on ultrasound alone. Your specialist can explain how the guidance applies to your situation.

Investigation is not always a rigid process of ruling out cancer first and considering everything else afterwards. Several possible causes may be assessed together. If bleeding continues or returns despite reassuring initial results, report it so that the plan can be reconsidered.

Lubricants, moisturisers and reducing irritation

When dryness contributes to symptoms, a lubricant can reduce friction during sexual activity. A vaginal moisturiser is used regularly according to its instructions to help with ongoing dryness. These products have different purposes and should not be treated as identical.

Choose products intended for the area and stop using one that causes irritation. A water-based or suitable silicone-based lubricant may be an option. Follow the instructions for condoms, diaphragms and sex toys, because material compatibility matters.

Oil-based products and petroleum jelly can damage latex or polyisoprene condoms and increase the chance of splitting. Do not assume a household cream or oil is safe for use with a barrier method.

Avoid douching and perfumed intimate products, and wash the external area gently. These steps can improve comfort but do not replace investigation of bleeding, treat every infection or guarantee that bleeding will never recur.

Hormone treatment and other cause-specific care

For menopause-related dryness, a clinician may discuss vaginal oestrogen, which is available in forms such as creams, tablets, pessaries or rings. Dosing and replacement intervals depend on the product; a ninety-day schedule applies to some rings, not every treatment.

Local treatment and systemic menopausal hormone therapy are different options with different uses and considerations. A systemic regimen is not automatically needed for vaginal symptoms. Discuss your medical history, unexplained bleeding and any history of hormone-sensitive cancer before starting treatment.

An identified infection may require antibiotics or another specific medicine. Complete the prescribed course and follow advice about partners and sexual contact if an STI is diagnosed. Antibiotics do not treat all forms of vaginitis, because some are not bacterial infections.

Symptomatic polyps may be removed and assessed. Persistent troublesome ectropion may sometimes be treated with silver nitrate, freezing or another procedure after appropriate checks. These are selected treatments for a confirmed condition, not a routine way to remove cells damaged by an untreated infection.

If testing identifies a precancerous change or cancer, specialist care is needed. The appropriate plan depends on the finding and its extent. A general article cannot choose the treatment or replace discussion of its benefits and risks.

Possible complications and follow-up

A few spots of blood do not usually cause anaemia. Repeated, prolonged or heavier bleeding can, however, contribute to iron deficiency. Fatigue, weakness, dizziness, headaches, breathlessness or unusual pallor are reasons to discuss whether blood testing is needed.

If iron deficiency is confirmed, care may include iron replacement as well as treating the source of blood loss. Iron-rich food is useful, but diet alone may not correct an established deficiency or explain why bleeding is occurring.

Dryness and menopause-related tissue changes can also accompany recurrent urinary symptoms or infections. Burning during urination, frequent urination or repeated suspected UTIs deserve their own assessment rather than being assumed to be caused by a small tear.

Many causes of bleeding after sex are treatable. Follow the agreed plan, and return if symptoms persist, worsen or recur. Improvement with lubrication is useful information, but it is not a diagnostic test that rules out other causes.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS guidance recommends checking unusual bleeding, including bleeding after sex, and distinguishes routine assessment from urgent symptoms such as a missed period with bleeding and abdominal pain. A normal screening result does not replace symptom assessment.

Treatment follows the cause. Guidance on dryness, ectropion and postmenopausal bleeding supports different approaches rather than one universal remedy; ACOG’s 2026 update also changes how many patients with postmenopausal bleeding are initially investigated.

How BeMama can help

Note when bleeding occurs, associated pain or discharge, medicines and previous test results. Bring that information to an appointment and ask what each recommended test is intended to answer.

When to seek help

Arrange assessment even for light bleeding after sex. Seek urgent care for heavy bleeding, severe pain, faintness or possible pregnancy complications. Do not start hormone treatment for unexplained bleeding without discussing it with a clinician.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Bleeding after sex often has a treatable cause, but even light bleeding should be checked.
  • Dryness, infection, cervical ectropion, polyps and injury are distinct possibilities with different treatments.
  • Any bleeding after menopause needs assessment; a normal cervical screen does not rule out every cause.
  • An examination can be planned with explanation, consent and adjustments for comfort.
  • Heavy bleeding, severe pain, faintness or possible pregnancy complications need urgent care.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need an appointment if it was only a small spot?

Yes. Arrange a check even if the bleeding was light or stopped quickly. It is often due to a treatable cause, but the amount alone cannot establish the explanation.

Is bleeding after menopause normal if it follows sex?

No. It should be assessed even if it happened once or you also have dryness. The clinician may need to examine the vaginal tissues and investigate the uterine lining.

Does bleeding after sex usually mean cancer?

No. Dryness, infection, ectropion, polyps and injury are other possible causes. Cancer is an important possibility to exclude when appropriate, which is why symptoms should not be dismissed.

Can a recent normal smear replace an assessment?

No. Routine cervical screening has a different purpose and does not check every possible source of bleeding. Tell a clinician about the symptom rather than waiting for the next screening appointment.

What if I am afraid of the pelvic examination?

Tell the service in advance. Ask for an explanation, a support person or chaperone, comfort adjustments and the option to pause. Some initial tests can be discussed first, but an examination may still be important for finding the cause.

Are a lubricant and a vaginal moisturiser the same thing?

No. A lubricant reduces friction during sexual activity, while a vaginal moisturiser is generally used regularly for ongoing dryness. Use products intended for the area and follow their instructions.

Can I use petroleum jelly with a condom?

Do not use petroleum jelly or other oil-based products with latex or polyisoprene condoms because they can damage the material. Check the barrier product’s instructions and choose a compatible lubricant.

Will antibiotics stop the bleeding?

Only when an infection that responds to them is the cause. Other explanations require different care. Do not self-treat every episode as an infection.

Does ectropion mean that my cervix has cancer or an untreated infection?

No. Ectropion is a common benign surface change. Infection and other abnormalities are checked before treatment is considered for persistent symptoms.

When should I seek urgent help?

Get urgent help for heavy or ongoing bleeding, severe pelvic or abdominal pain, faintness, collapse or feeling very unwell. A missed period with bleeding and abdominal pain could be an ectopic pregnancy and needs urgent assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
